page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard4.Ax.Flex.2-16 is a general-purpose virtual machine based on the x86_64 architecture. It is powered by an Intel Xeon 6987C-P processor operating at 3.9 GHz with dedicated CPU core allocation. The instance provisions 2 physical cores with 2 threads per core, yielding 4 dedicated virtual CPUs paired with 16.0 GB of memory. This maintains a standard general-purpose ratio of 4.0 GB of RAM per vCPU.

Hardware acceleration is not included, with GPU count standing at zero. Additionally, the instance provides no integrated local disk storage, necessitating the attachment of remote block volumes for persistent filesystem needs and OS operations. Network connectivity includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. The provision of dedicated CPU resources avoids resource contention across physical execution threads.

The 1:4 compute-to-memory configuration delivers a balanced profile suited for workloads that require stable CPU clock rates without high memory density or dedicated accelerator cards. It offers a cost-effective operational profile for mid-tier web servers, backend application microservices, development environments, and small relational database instances dependent on external persistent storage.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard4.Ax.Flex.2-16 is a general-purpose virtual machine configured with 4 vCPUs across 2 physical cores and 16.0 GB of system memory. Driven by a dedicated Intel Xeon 6987C-P processor with x86_64 architecture operating at 3.9 GHz, it maintains a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-memory allocation. The shape does not include local disk storage or GPU accelerators, relying on network-attached block storage for system files and persistent data. One complimentary public IPv4 address is assigned. Due to its dedicated CPU mapping, the instance prevents hypervisor-level CPU contention across its execution threads. This hardware profile provides a resource-efficient baseline for steady-state enterprise application hosting, microservices, container clusters, continuous integration workers, and light database deployments.
